name: FSH / Menopur (HMG)

card.summary: Fertility gonadotropins (FSH, hMG) from IVF medicine, discussed in TRT circles as a way to keep sperm production going; the evidence is in women's fertility, not appearance.
card.aka: Menopur, menotropin, human menopausal gonadotropin, hMG, Pergonal
card.note: Prescription fertility drugs with monitoring requirements; trial evidence is mostly in women undergoing IVF.

quick.overview:
Menopur is a brand of highly purified menotropin (human menopausal gonadotropin, hMG), a mixture of FSH and LH activity originally extracted from the urine of postmenopausal women. It is used to stimulate the ovaries in fertility treatment, and the same drug class can be used in hypogonadal men to stimulate sperm production.

In looksmaxxing and TRT communities these gonadotropins come up as fertility-preserving companions to testosterone therapy. The published trials are almost all in women having IVF, and none examine appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: FSH acts on ovarian follicles in women and on Sertoli cells in men to support gamete production, while LH activity stimulates sex-hormone production. Menopur supplies both activities; recombinant FSH products supply FSH alone.
quick.risks: Known concerns in women's fertility treatment include ovarian overstimulation and multiple pregnancy. These are prescription drugs given by injection under monitoring. Specific harms in men using them alongside testosterone are not covered by the trials listed here.

lead: Menotropin, also called human menopausal gonadotropin (hMG), is a fertility drug extracted from the urine of postmenopausal women, whose urine is rich in FSH and LH [1]. Menopur, made by Ferring, is a highly purified preparation; earlier products included Pergonal [1]. In women it is used to stimulate follicle growth for IVF; in hypogonadal men it can be used to stimulate sperm production [1].

In muscle and testosterone-therapy communities, FSH and hMG are discussed as companions to testosterone replacement. The chain people describe runs: exogenous testosterone suppresses the brain's LH and FSH signals, which lowers sperm production and testicular size; adding gonadotropin activity keeps the testes working, so users keep fertility and the fuller testicular volume that they associate with a natural look [15][16][17]. Any appearance link is therefore indirect and claimed rather than studied.

The extraction method was developed by Piero Donini in 1949 and brought into clinical use by Bruno Lunenfeld in 1961 [1]. Wikipedia notes recombinant FSH has largely replaced hMG in many settings and that a Cochrane analysis found no major clinical outcome differences between urinary and recombinant FSH [1]. Trial evidence is concentrated in women undergoing IVF or ovulation induction [2][3][4][19][20].

paras: Menotropin preparations contain FSH and LH activity, with small amounts of hCG and other proteins. Early products such as Pergonal held FSH and LH in a 1:1 ratio; because FSH is considered the main driver of follicle stimulation, later preparations were developed with a higher FSH-to-LH ratio [1]. Menopur is described in a 2018 review as a highly purified, urine-derived hMG with both FSH and LH activity [19].

Preparations marketed over time include Pergonal, Repronex, Menopur, Merional, Humegon, Gynogen HP and others [1]. Wikipedia notes a theoretical risk of infection from the urine source, which it describes as unsupported by experimental findings [1].

Donini's 1949 extraction method for urinary gonadotropins and Lunenfeld's 1961 introduction of hMG into clinical use made menotropin the main ovulation-stimulating drug of the following decades [1]. Pergonal was the principal hMG product before recombinant gonadotropins arrived [1].

Recombinant FSH and LH later allowed production of single hormones without other urinary proteins. Head-to-head studies of purified FSH against hMG have been mixed, and the American Society for Reproductive Medicine has reported no confirmed differences in safety, purity or clinical efficacy among available urinary and recombinant products, according to Wikipedia [1].

In women it is used to stimulate follicle growth for IVF and ovulation induction, with daily injections over roughly ten days under close monitoring [1]. A 2018 review calls Menopur an effective option for controlled ovarian stimulation and for ovulation induction in anovulatory infertility [19]. In hypogonadal men it can be used to stimulate sperm production [1]. A case report describes a birth after testicular sperm extraction in a man with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism [8].

Forum participants describe FSH or hMG being added to hCG by men on TRT who want better sperm counts. One T Nation poster says a physician prescribed Menopur to give Sertoli cells a boost and that insurance would not cover recombinant FSH [16]; another says that adding FSH took their sperm concentration above a fertility threshold where hCG alone had not [15]. Another poster in a thread on TRT and hCG says that adding hCG and FSH gives the best chance of fertility on TRT and reports having seen men move from about 5 million to 50 to 80 million sperm [17]. A poster in a separate thread describes the cost of a few months of Menopur as high compared with hCG [18].
These are individual reports. The published trials of Menopur listed here are in women having IVF or insemination.

A randomised, assessor-blind multinational trial in 731 women compared highly purified hMG (Menopur) with recombinant FSH (Gonal-F) in IVF, reporting ongoing pregnancy rates of 27 percent with hMG versus 22 percent with rFSH [5]. A companion analysis examined embryo quality [5], and an endocrine analysis found different serum and follicular-fluid profiles between the two products [12].

A 2010 meta-analysis of five randomized trials found similar ongoing pregnancy and live-birth rates between Menopur and Gonal-F, concluding the combined data did not support clinical superiority of Gonal-F [20]. A 2020 randomized trial in 620 predicted high responders reported ongoing pregnancy rates of 35.5 percent with hMG and 30.7 percent with rFSH, establishing noninferiority, with lower ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome with hMG (9.7 percent versus 21.4 percent) [21].

A trial in poor responders compared 450 IU and 600 IU gonadotropin dosing [6], and a randomised trial compared low-dose hMG with clomiphene in subfertile couples having intrauterine insemination [7]. Economic evaluations of two large trials compared hMG and rFSH costs [9].

The main known concerns in women's fertility treatment are ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome and multiple pregnancy; the 2020 high-responder trial reported OHSS rates for each arm [21]. A randomized IVF study of 125 women found fewer injection-site reactions with Menopur than with Repronex, with no difference in overall adverse events [22]. Harms in men using gonadotropins alongside testosterone are not covered by these trials.

Urinary preparations contain impurities in addition to gonadotropins, which has been analysed in the literature [10]. Studies have also compared batch-to-batch consistency of human-derived and recombinant gonadotropin products [11]. A 2021 trial reported a liquid pre-filled-pen formulation of Menopur to be bioequivalent to the powder form [23].

Menopur and related products are prescription-only. Brand names include Menopur, Pergonal, Repronex, Merional, Humegon, Menogon and Gynogen HP [1]. In TRT forums, posters discuss gonadotropin use as part of fertility regimens run with clinicians or by themselves, and the topic often appears in threads on hCG [15][16][17].

Large trials in women show comparative outcomes between hMG and rFSH in IVF [5][12][20][21], with additional Phase 3 and 4 registrations of Menopur in infertility, including a 270-patient IVF safety and efficacy study [13] and a 620-patient single-blastocyst transfer study in high responders [14]. A 2025 randomized trial compared two highly purified hMG products [24]. No studies found examining FSH or hMG for appearance outcomes or for men using them alongside testosterone therapy.

timeline.event: Piero Donini develops an extraction method for urinary gonadotropins [1].
Bruno Lunenfeld introduces hMG into clinical use [1].

lore.intro: On T Nation and similar forums, FSH and hMG appear in threads about preserving fertility and testicular function on testosterone therapy [15][16][17].

claims.claim: Adding FSH to hCG raises sperm counts in men on TRT
claims.believers: Posters report men moving from low to much higher sperm concentrations after adding FSH, and one says FSH is what stimulates sperm production [15][17].
claims.experts: FSH acts on Sertoli cells and menotropin is used to stimulate sperm production in hypogonadal men [1]. The trials of Menopur cited here are in women, and none test men on testosterone therapy.

claims.claim: Menopur is a practical source of FSH activity when recombinant FSH is not covered
claims.believers: A poster says a physician prescribed Menopur because insurance would not cover rFSH [16]; another notes the monthly cost is far higher than hCG [18].
claims.experts: Comparative IVF trials found similar pregnancy rates between hMG and recombinant FSH [20][21], and ASRM has reported no confirmed differences in efficacy among available products [1].

angle.goal: Testicular function and fertility on testosterone therapy
chain: Testosterone therapy suppresses LH and FSH
Sperm production and testicular volume fall
Gonadotropin activity (hCG, FSH, hMG) is added by some users
Spermatogenesis supported; testicular size kept closer to baseline
angle.text: Men on TRT who want to keep fertility, or who prefer to avoid testicular shrinkage, discuss FSH and hMG as a way to keep the testes stimulated. Users describe this mainly as fertility insurance; it is not a muscle or physique agent itself.
